chapter.name: Continuity and Differentiability
chapter.blurb: Continuity of a real function at a point and on its domain, the algebra and composition of continuous functions, and differentiability with its link to continuity (every differentiable function is continuous, but not conversely). The chapter then builds differentiation techniques: the chain rule, implicit differentiation, derivatives of inverse trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions, logarithmic differentiation, parametric forms and second order derivatives.

scope_in.item: State the definition of continuity at x = c (lim (x -> c) f(x) = f(c)) and test it by comparing left hand limit, right hand limit and f(c)
Check continuity at a point for polynomial, modulus and piecewise-defined functions, and find every point of discontinuity of a piecewise function
Find the value of a constant (k, lambda, a, b) that makes a piecewise function continuous at a given point
Recognise a continuous function as one continuous at every point of its own domain, including end points of [a, b] via one-sided limits, and explain why 1/x is continuous though its graph breaks at 0
Interpret lim (x -> 0+) 1/x = +infinity and lim (x -> 0-) 1/x = -infinity, recognising infinity is not a real number so these limits do not exist

Show that constant, identity, polynomial, rational, modulus, sine, cosine and tangent functions are continuous on their domains, and that the greatest integer function is discontinuous at every integer
Use the algebra of continuous functions (f + g, f - g, f . g, f/g with g(c) != 0, lambda f, 1/g) and the composite-function theorem to decide continuity
Use the definition f'(c) = lim (h -> 0) [f(c + h) - f(c)]/h, with left and right hand derivatives, to decide differentiability at a point, and on [a, b] or (a, b)
State and use Theorem 3 (differentiable implies continuous) and show the converse fails using |x| at 0, |x - 1| at 1 and [x] at integers
Recall standard derivatives of x^n, sin x, cos x, tan x and the sum, product and quotient rules
Differentiate composite functions with the chain rule, including its extension to three functions
Differentiate implicit relations between x and y term by term, applying the chain rule to y-terms

Derive and use d/dx sin^(-1) x = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2), d/dx cos^(-1) x = -1/sqrt(1 - x^2) (on (-1, 1)) and d/dx tan^(-1) x = 1/(1 + x^2), including substitutions such as x = tan t to simplify before differentiating

State properties of the exponential function b^x (b > 1) and the logarithm log_b x (domain, range, points (0, 1) and (1, 0), increasing, mirror images in y = x), define e^x and natural log, and use log laws and change of base
Use d/dx (e^x) = e^x and d/dx (log x) = 1/x with the chain rule
Differentiate [u(x)]^(v(x)), products, quotients and roots by logarithmic differentiation, including d/dx (a^x) = a^x log a and sums of such terms
Find dy/dx for parametric forms x = f(t), y = g(t) as (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), dx/dt != 0, and differentiate one function with respect to another
Find second order derivatives d^2y/dx^2 (notations f''(x), D^2 y, y'', y_2) and use them to verify given relations such as d^2y/dx^2 + y = 0

concepts.name: Continuity at a point and points of discontinuity
concepts.description: Testing whether f is continuous at x = c by comparing the left hand limit, right hand limit and value f(c), including piecewise functions, finding a constant that makes f continuous, and locating points of discontinuity.
concepts.idea: A function is continuous at a point if its graph can be drawn through that point without lifting the pen; precisely, the limit of f at c must equal the value f(c).
concepts.rule: f is continuous at x = c when f(c) is defined and lim (x -> c-) f(x) = lim (x -> c+) f(x) = f(c). If any of these fails, c is a point of discontinuity.
concepts.example: f(x) = x + 2 for x <= 1 and x - 2 for x > 1: the left hand limit at 1 is 3 and the right hand limit is -1, so x = 1 is the only point of discontinuity.

concepts.name: Continuous functions, algebra and composition of continuous functions
concepts.description: Recognising continuous functions (constant, identity, polynomial, rational, modulus, sine, cosine, tangent), using the sum, difference, product and quotient theorem and the composite-function theorem to decide continuity.
concepts.idea: A function is continuous if it is continuous at every point of its own domain, and continuity is preserved when continuous functions are added, subtracted, multiplied, divided (where the denominator is non-zero) or composed.
concepts.rule: If f and g are continuous at c, then f + g, f - g, f . g and f/g (g(c) != 0) are continuous at c. If g is continuous at c and f is continuous at g(c), then f o g is continuous at c.
concepts.example: sin (x^2) is continuous because it is g o h with g(x) = sin x and h(x) = x^2, both continuous; 1/x is continuous because 0 is not in its domain.

concepts.name: Differentiability and its relation to continuity
concepts.description: The derivative as lim (h -> 0) [f(c + h) - f(c)]/h, differentiability at a point via equal finite left and right hand derivatives, and the theorem that differentiability implies continuity but not conversely.
concepts.idea: A function is differentiable at c when the slope limit [f(c + h) - f(c)]/h settles to one finite value from both sides; a corner or a break stops this.
concepts.rule: f is differentiable at c if lim (h -> 0-) [f(c + h) - f(c)]/h and lim (h -> 0+) [f(c + h) - f(c)]/h are finite and equal. Every differentiable function is continuous; the converse is false.
concepts.example: f(x) = |x| is continuous at 0, but its left hand derivative there is -1 and its right hand derivative is 1, so it is not differentiable at 0.

questions.q: Does there exist a function which is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at exactly two points? Justify using f(x) = |x| + |x - 1|.
questions.a: Yes. f = |x| + |x - 1| is a sum of continuous functions, so it is continuous everywhere. Written piecewise: f = 1 - 2x for x < 0, f = 1 for 0 <= x <= 1, f = 2x - 1 for x > 1. At x = 0 the left hand derivative is -2 and the right hand derivative is 0; at x = 1 the left hand derivative is 0 and the right hand derivative is 2. So f is not differentiable at exactly x = 0 and x = 1, and is differentiable everywhere else.
s: Answers yes and states f is continuous everywhere as a sum of continuous functions
Shows the left and right hand derivatives differ at x = 0 (-2 and 0)
Shows they differ at x = 1 (0 and 2), and that these are the only two such points

questions.q: A student claims: 'The graph of f(x) = |x| can be drawn without lifting the pen, so f is differentiable everywhere.' Evaluate the claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Drawing without lifting the pen shows continuity, not differentiability. At x = 0 the left hand derivative of |x| is -1 and the right hand derivative is 1, so |x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0.
s: Explains that the pen test shows only continuity, and continuity does not imply differentiability

concepts.name: Second order derivatives
concepts.description: Finding d^2y/dx^2 by differentiating dy/dx again, its notations (f''(x), D^2 y, y'', y_2), and using it to verify relations such as d^2y/dx^2 + y = 0.
concepts.idea: The second order derivative is the derivative of the derivative: it measures how dy/dx itself changes with x.
concepts.rule: d^2y/dx^2 = d/dx (dy/dx), written f''(x), D^2 y, y'' or y_2; it exists where f'(x) is differentiable.
concepts.example: y = x^3 + tan x: dy/dx = 3x^2 + sec^2 x, so d^2y/dx^2 = 6x + 2 sec^2 x tan x.
